Lu Wenfeng unfastens the sheath and takes out an item in the riverside private room, pushing the ebony boat token wrapped in oilcloth to Liu Sanniang—an old grain-transport seal on the front, a newly carved character “seven” on the back—and presses her about what was loaded on the seventh-ranked boat at Qixia Ferry that year.

Liu Sanniang turns the lampwick down, lifts the cloth through a handkerchief, verifies that the old grain-transport seal is genuine and that the hidden fish-tail mark is the mark for escorting internal cargo back then, and accepts the boat plaque.

Liu Sanniang for the first time explains the true cargo of Qixia Ferry’s seventh boat—three tin boxes (official silver, salt certificates, and private toll accounts), with a Mr. Qi, an accountant from the Grain Transport Supervision Office, hidden in the bottom of the cabin together with his tri-border draft register; she also points out that the fire was set to seize the accounts and silence him, and asserts that this tag is a death warrant.

Lu Wenfeng takes out the second piece of physical evidence—the wax-sealed paper roll taken from behind the corpse's teeth, with 'the seven boats' accounts are at Banhuchun Inn' written on it—drawing the fire of the old case to the lintel of Liu Sanniang's own inn, and questioning her face-to-face about the names of the three people with cable wounds.

Liu Sanniang pressed down on the paper roll and did not break the sealing wax. For the first time, she personally acknowledged the name of the second mate of the Seventh Boat — Han Bozhou, nicknamed "Sanlanzi"; the three rope scars on his left wrist were twisted out back when they crossed the Meisha rapids.

Liu Sanniang pointed out that the words “the seven-ship ledger is at Banhuchun” on the wax pill were meant for someone familiar to see—someone knew that she recognized ship plaques, and also knew Lu Wenfeng would send the thing to her. She further asserted that Banhuchun did not have that death-bringing ledger; if the ledger truly was in the building, then it was either a frame-up, or the insider from back then was still not dead.

Lu Wenfeng holds down Liu Sanniang’s hand as she is about to break the wax, points out that green sand mixed into the sealing wax is the old rule by which the grain-transport gang passes death notices, and advances the questioning from “identifying the person” to “besides Han Bozhou, who else back then knew you were at Banhuchun Inn”—turning “the mole” from speculation into a question that must be answered face to face, and pointing directly at Liu Sanniang’s deepest taboo.

Liu Sanniang does not struggle when her hand is held down; she withdraws her fingertips, covers the paper roll and the ebony boat token together with a handkerchief, and pushes them three inches away from the lamplight, pointing out the old rule of Qingsha sealing death notices: if it is opened too early, the messenger’s life-intent will be cut off halfway.

Regarding “who else knows you are at Banhuchun Inn,” Liu Sanniang gives the list of people who knew back then: Han Bozhou; Shen Qingshan, the former accountant of the Cao Gang (Iron Abacus, rumored to have died in Huaibei five years ago but with no corpse ever found); and Qin Zhaoshui, the old helmsman (stricken by stroke for seven years, unless someone is borrowing his name).

Liu Sanniang asserts that, apart from Han Bozhou, the person most worth investigating is Shen Qingshan—if Iron Abacus is still alive, he knows about the seventh boat and also about Banhuchun; if he is dead, then someone has taken his old accounts, old seals, and old favors to play ghost.

Liu Sanniang presses the window latch even tighter and asks Lu Wenfeng in return: who took this wax pellet from behind Han Bozhou’s teeth—did he take it out with his own hands, or did someone pass it into her hands?

Lu Wenfeng answers, “I took it out with my own hands”—the old boatman who fished up the body only touched the lapel and never saw the wax pill; from the time he took it out until he reached Banhuchun Inn, the chain of custody for the wax pill narrowed to him alone. He then releases Liu Sanniang’s hand, advancing the inquiry from “who wrote it” to “if Shen Qingshan is still alive, what old mark would be recognizable at a glance”—the investigation advances from “counting heads” to “finding a person.”

Liu Sanniang states three old identifying marks of Shen Qingshan: the horizontal callus on the inner side of his left thumb worn by abacus beads; that when working the abacus he favored the three fingers of his left hand, and when doing “two and five return to one” his middle finger would strike one extra time; a blue-black mole behind his right ear (“Qingshan carrying ink”); and that when writing the character “Shen,” the final dot always hooked back (because an old injury to his right wrist made his finishing stroke unable to close straight). She also wipes clean the water marks on the table with a handkerchief and arranges for Lu Wenfeng to rest tonight in the elegant room by the river; at daybreak, Afu will go to the river wharf to ask about the background of the old boatman from Wupeng Bay, while Lu Wenfeng will not show himself.
attention: Liu Sanniang: He answered crisply—he took it with his own hands; the old boatman only touched the lapel. The last bit of suspense in her heart also settled: from the dead man's mouth to his hands, this wax pellet passed through no third hand. She trusts that he will not sell this question on to someone else, and also trusts that when he asks now about Shen Qingshan's mark, it is because he wants to investigate further, not because he wants to use her as bait.

Liu Sanniang: He asks what old mark on Shen Qingshan could be recognized at a glance—as soon as these words fall, that ledger in her mind turns another page. This time it turns to the face of Iron Abacus from twelve years ago: the horizontal callus on his left thumb, the blue mole behind his right ear, and the little point where he hooks back when writing the character “Shen.” The more detailed her answer, the clearer she becomes: the more accurately she recognizes him, the more it shows how close this person was to her back then.

Liu Sanniang: Toward the person before her, she has not the slightest resentment in her heart—this question of his is helping her turn the blade toward Shen Qingshan, not toward her. What she is still angry at is the hand that wrote “Banhuchun” into the wax pellet and used Han Bozhou’s corpse to pass a message to the living.

Liu Sanniang: After half a year apart, as soon as he returns he lays before her, one by one, the things taken from a dead man's mouth; he even answers bluntly to words like “taken by my own hand”, and now he asks what mark Shen Qingshan has—this person truly has not treated her as an outsider, and so she is even less willing to let him go on alone.

Liu Sanniang: not only has the chest in her heart been opened, but beneath the sheet at the bottom of the chest bearing her own shop’s name, there is also an even colder line pressed underneath: the person who wrote this line may be someone she knows, and may still be alive. What she fears is no longer only the account book from back then, but these twelve years of Banhuchun—Afu, Lao Zhao, those old faces by the river—which one of them sold out her place of refuge?

Liu Sanniang: This question is enough to make anyone jump up, but she does not. His hand is holding hers down, and she does not struggle; her words are pressed low enough for only the two of them to hear, while the clinking of wine cups downstairs goes on as usual. The rule of twelve years—the hotter the words are to handle, the more slowly they must be said.

Liu Sanniang: The two forces in her heart twisted even tighter—if she answers with Shen Qingshan’s mark, she is placing, one by one, those old faces that are still alive after all these years under the lamp; but if she does not answer, does not acknowledge it, she is pushing back, right in front of Lu Wenfeng, the relationship she has just accepted. She answered Han Bozhou; now what she has to answer concerns the living—this threshold is higher than that tablet just now.

Liu Sanniang: When he answers, "I took it with my own hands," that bit of suspense in her heart also settles—but this makes her want even more to know who stuffed this wax pellet into Han Bozhou's mouth. She understands the layer of green sand as soon as she hears it—an old rule for transmitting news of death, not something outsiders can imitate. She even wants to examine the seal closely by the lamp to see whether any fingerprints were left on it.

Liu Sanniang: she had never even mentioned the three words “Qixia Ferry” to Afu. Now it is not only being brought up to her face; someone has dredged that batch of old boat tags up from the bottom of the water, written “Banhuchun Inn” into a wax pellet, and also wants her to count out with her own mouth who knew about it back then and identify Shen Qingshan's mark. The old wound has been uncovered, and she still has to hold it down herself, pressing harder than before.

Liu Sanniang: He answered, ‘I took it with my own hands,’ and as soon as she heard that, she understood: mixing green sand into wax was an old rule of the canal gang for passing on news of a death, not something an outsider could imitate. The person who wrote this wax pellet was someone inside the canal gang, and knew that she was staying at Banhuchun and knew that Lu Wenfeng would come looking for her. This was not digging up old accounts; it was using the dead to pass a message to the living, and the opening of that message pointed straight at someone she knew.

Liu Sanniang: She names Han Bozhou, Shen Qingshan, and Qin Zhaoshui, points the spearhead at Shen Qingshan, and then hands the thread of the conversation back to Lu Wenfeng—how far to answer, and toward which name to lead it, are still for her to decide.

Lu Wenfeng: He has also explained the entire process of handling the wax pellet—he took it with his own hands; the old boatman only touched his lapel, and it passed through no second person along the way. He even says such a critical sentence as “I was the only one who handled this line” to her face. There is not much left for him to hide from her.

Lu Wenfeng: His hand loosened, but the string in his heart did not. What he asked was not “where is Shen Qingshan,” but “what old mark can be recognized at a glance”—he is preparing to identify someone, which means he intends to personally go and dig this person out of the shadows.

Lu Wenfeng: He has not the slightest hostility toward the old shopkeeper. He lets go of her hand and asks about an old mark; the blade is aimed at Shen Qingshan’s hand that may be pretending to be a ghost.

Lu Wenfeng: Half a year without seeing her, and the moment he returns he lays out before her, one by one, the things taken from a dead man's mouth; now he has even said words like "taken by my own hand, passed through no hands but mine." This kind of bond is not made through pleasantries; it is traded into being, one object at a time.

Lu Wenfeng: The wax pellet passed through only his hands, so the line “The seven boats’ accounts are at Banhuchun” can only have been written for him, and for her—the person who knows this thread is among the three names she just counted out. The room is quieter than before.

Lu Wenfeng: He wants the answer, yet fears that answer coming from her mouth—asking “what old mark did Shen Qingshan have” is asking her to hand over another layer of the details of her former comrade. This threshold is higher than that plaque just now.

Lu Wenfeng: what the seventh boat carried, why the fire started, what the newly carved character “seven” meant, where the accounts were, who was injured by the three cable marks, the old rule that seal wax mixed with green sand conveys a death notice, who knew about it back then, and whose hands the wax pellet passed through—all eight items are complete. He has felt out the full skeleton of this old case.

paths.summary: Taking the chance to close the window in the elegant room by the river, the two advance the topic from “counting heads” to “identifying Shen Qingshan and investigating the handler of the wax pill”—Liu Sanniang explains the distinguishable features of the Shen Qingshan lead, and Lu Wenfeng adds the source of the corpse and the course by which the wax pill changed hands. Their connection resumes; Liu Sanniang probes out some of the direction, Lu Wenfeng also gets hold of the thread, and they may reach a tacit understanding about the next step.

original.rationale: In this turn, Liu Sanniang has already spoken aloud the core secret she kept for twelve years, the specific names, and the list of those in the know, leaving herself no way back; Lu Wenfeng came with the corpse, the boat token, and the wax pellet precisely to reconcile accounts, and now he has even exposed the old rules of Qingsha and pushed the questioning toward the list of those in the know and identifying features. Both sides have already gone upstairs, the scene is set, and the groundwork has been handed over at this level; the most likely path is to continue digging deeper along this line.

evidence.quote: I opened the ledger, my fingertip sliding down along the room accounts for the past half month, my voice kept very steady: “Banhuchun Inn has its rules. Guests’ names and room numbers—I don’t sell those to outsiders. But if someone is trying to splash the dirty water of the ‘Seven-Boat Accounts’ through my door, then he is no ordinary passerby. He is coming for my signboard.”

“Three days ago, there was a man who stayed here claiming to be a silk merchant from Huaibei. When he came in, his clothes were clean, but the soles of his shoes had river mud on them; he didn’t look as if he had come by land. When he settled the bill, he complained that Afu was too slow with the abacus, and reached out to flick it twice himself—three fingers of his left hand, with the middle finger striking one extra time.”

“There was another thing. When he registered, he didn’t write the surname as ‘沈’; he wrote ‘申,’ the shen of the shen hour. His name was Shen He. But the last stroke hooked back, like a fishhook drawing in the line.”
I gave a cold laugh and shut the ledger. “I told him Banhuchun keeps wine for people, not lives.”

“Don’t alarm the old boatman for now. I’ll have Afu go to the wharf tomorrow to buy fish and keep an eye out in passing. As for this ‘Shen He’—if he really is Iron Abacus, then since he asked about the trunks, that means he doesn’t know where the accounts are either. He is searching, and so are we. But we cannot let him know that we have already woken up.”

Liu Sanniang does not struggle when her hand is held down; she withdraws her fingertips, covers the paper roll and the ebony boat token together with a handkerchief, and pushes them three inches away from the lamplight, pointing out the old rule of Qingsha sealing death notices: if it is opened too early, the messenger’s life-intent will be cut off halfway.

Regarding “who else knows you are at Banhuchun Inn,” Liu Sanniang gives the list of people who knew back then: Han Bozhou; Shen Qingshan, the former accountant of the Cao Gang (Iron Abacus, rumored to have died in Huaibei five years ago but with no corpse ever found); and Qin Zhaoshui, the old helmsman (stricken by stroke for seven years, unless someone is borrowing his name).

Liu Sanniang asserts that, apart from Han Bozhou, the person most worth investigating is Shen Qingshan—if Iron Abacus is still alive, he knows about the seventh boat and also about Banhuchun; if he is dead, then someone has taken his old accounts, old seals, and old favors to play ghost.

Liu Sanniang presses the window latch even tighter and asks Lu Wenfeng in return: who took this wax pellet from behind Han Bozhou’s teeth—did he take it out with his own hands, or did someone pass it into her hands?

Lu Wenfeng answers, “I took it out with my own hands”—the old boatman who fished up the body only touched the lapel and never saw the wax pill; from the time he took it out until he reached Banhuchun Inn, the chain of custody for the wax pill narrowed to him alone. He then releases Liu Sanniang’s hand, advancing the inquiry from “who wrote it” to “if Shen Qingshan is still alive, what old mark would be recognizable at a glance”—the investigation advances from “counting heads” to “finding a person.”

Liu Sanniang states three old identifying marks of Shen Qingshan: the horizontal callus on the inner side of his left thumb worn by abacus beads; that when working the abacus he favored the three fingers of his left hand, and when doing “two and five return to one” his middle finger would strike one extra time; a blue-black mole behind his right ear (“Qingshan carrying ink”); and that when writing the character “Shen,” the final dot always hooked back (because an old injury to his right wrist made his finishing stroke unable to close straight). She also wipes clean the water marks on the table with a handkerchief and arranges for Lu Wenfeng to rest tonight in the elegant room by the river; at daybreak, Afu will go to the river wharf to ask about the background of the old boatman from Wupeng Bay, while Lu Wenfeng will not show himself.

Lu Wenfeng puts the boat plaque and wax pellet away again, asks that they not alert the old boatman yet and only keep watch for now, and advances the questioning from “what marks does Shen Qingshan have” to “among those who have stayed at the inn recently, is there anyone who works an abacus with the left hand, or writes the character “Shen” with a hook”—feeding the already obtained identifying features back into an in-house screening. The investigation advances from “looking for someone” to “comparing within one’s own hall”.

Liu Sanniang opens the room accounts from nearly the past half month and recognizes a suspicious man who stayed at the inn three days ago: he claimed to be a silk merchant from Huaibei, had river mud on the soles of his shoes, used three fingers of his left hand to move the abacus when settling the bill and tapped an extra time with his middle finger, wrote the final stroke of the character "申" in the register with a hook like a fishhook, stayed only one night before leaving by the small rear-river dock, and before leaving had asked, "Are there any trunks left in storage by people from the old grain-transport gang?"—three identifying marks collide in one place, and the target takes shape in her own hall.

Liu Sanniang refuses that person’s probing with “Banhuchun only sends wine, not lives,” and sets the tempo: do not alarm the old boatman yet; only have A Fu go to the wharf tomorrow to buy fish while keeping an eye out. If “Shen He” really is Iron Abacus, then since he has asked about the trunks, it means he also does not know where the accounts are—he is looking, and so are we, but we cannot let him know we have already awakened.

Lu Wenfeng advances the questioning from “recognizing features” to “checking physical evidence and the scene”—he wants that page of accounts, wants to see the room that person stayed in, and wants to check whether that person touched any old objects in the shop before leaving, advancing the investigation from “comparing features” to “turning over physical evidence and verifying the scene.”

Liu Sanniang opens the account book and shows only the line for “Shen He,” making clear that Earth Room No. 3 is by the back river, with a small dock right below the window; he will stay one night, the room fee is one qian, dinner requires only plain rice, salted fish, and hot tea, and when settling the bill, his left hand will move the abacus while his middle finger taps once more than usual.

Liu Sanniang recognizes that the person touched two old objects—the old abacus on the counter that Shen Qingshan left behind when he bought the shop back then (the third bead from the far left has been reversed), and the old bronze boat lamp dismantled from an old boat at Qixia Ferry at the stairway corner (on the inner side of the lamp belly there is an extra shallow scratch like a “seven” and like a fishhook). She asserts that this is a mark left for an accomplice: “the route has been found”.

Liu Sanniang closes the account book, lowers the lamp shade, and takes Lu Wenfeng to see Di No. 3, laying down the rule: “Looking is looking; don’t go rummaging through the bedboards. Banhuchun Inn still has business to do.”

plot_point: Regular customer Lu Wenfeng returns to the inn. Under the conditions that the hall is seventy percent full and only one Tian-class room remains, Liu Sanniang completes the full arrangement of reserving the room, ordering dishes, warming wine, quoting the price, and recording the account, and settles five qian and six wen (with one wen left as account credit).

Lu Wenfeng advances the topic from “is all still peaceful” to “old waves are rising again,” and asks Liu Sanniang whether any old members of the Canal Gang have recently come asking about Qixia Crossing.

Liu Sanniang does not answer directly; with “tea may be hot, but words should not be”, she lowers her voice, arranges for Lu Wenfeng to go upstairs and shut the window before speaking further, and offers half a piece of the truth: in the past month, a few old faces have been loitering by the river, asking indirect questions, as if probing how many people from that boat back then are still left.
Liu Sanniang reiterates the rule of “not selling to officials, not selling to the jianghu”, and in turn probes what Lu Wenfeng heard on the road.

Lu Wenfeng responds with “the dead have spoken”—three days ago, a corpse was recovered from Wupeng Bay, with the old boat plaques from that batch at Qixia Ferry hidden on the body; he proposes waiting until they finish eating and go upstairs to discuss it in detail, and uses “if you still recognize the old secret marks of the canal gang” to ask Liu Sanniang to reclaim her former identity.

Liu Sanniang catches the heavy words; first she raises her voice and orders Afu to light the lamps, test the window latches, and bring hot water, drawing the conversation in the front hall to a close, then personally pours wine and, with “using the dead to pass words to the living,” lays bare the purpose of the boat tag surfacing.

Liu Sanniang, for the first time, directly claims her old identity in the grain-transport gang—"I recognize the secret marks on the boat plaques"—and arranges to go upstairs after Lu Wenfeng finishes eating, using her taking the account book up as the pretext.
Liu Sanniang asks back in turn: Was this corpse aimed at Lu Wenfeng, or at the people from Qixia Ferry who didn’t die cleanly back then?

Lu Wenfeng reveals another piece of detail about the corpse—the three old cable scars on the left wrist, "as if from someone who survived on the boat back then"; he also proactively suggests "closing the door tightly first," and wants to go upstairs to show Liu Sanniang "something."

Liu Sanniang catches “three old cable wounds”, quietly agrees to go upstairs to eat, and orders A'Fu to watch the front hall, turn the stair lamp low, and stew ginger soup to be sent to the door, sealing off both the eyes and ears in the hall and the route upstairs.

Using the account book as a pretext, Liu Sanniang quietly laid down the rules to Lu Wenfeng: “do not ask where one comes from, and no drawing blades inside the building.” Then she went upstairs into the riverside private room, lit the lamp, shut the window, slid the bolt, carefully inspected the door crack, spread out the account book and set an abacus on it, adopting the posture of settling accounts, and asked Lu Wenfeng to take out that “one thing.”

Lu Wenfeng unfastens the sheath and takes out an item in the riverside private room, pushing the ebony boat token wrapped in oilcloth to Liu Sanniang—an old grain-transport seal on the front, a newly carved character “seven” on the back—and presses her about what was loaded on the seventh-ranked boat at Qixia Ferry that year.

Liu Sanniang turns the lampwick down, lifts the cloth through a handkerchief, verifies that the old grain-transport seal is genuine and that the hidden fish-tail mark is the mark for escorting internal cargo back then, and accepts the boat plaque.

Liu Sanniang for the first time explains the true cargo of Qixia Ferry’s seventh boat—three tin boxes (official silver, salt certificates, and private toll accounts), with a Mr. Qi, an accountant from the Grain Transport Supervision Office, hidden in the bottom of the cabin together with his tri-border draft register; she also points out that the fire was set to seize the accounts and silence him, and asserts that this tag is a death warrant.

Lu Wenfeng takes out the second piece of physical evidence—the wax-sealed paper roll taken from behind the corpse's teeth, with 'the seven boats' accounts are at Banhuchun Inn' written on it—drawing the fire of the old case to the lintel of Liu Sanniang's own inn, and questioning her face-to-face about the names of the three people with cable wounds.

Liu Sanniang pressed down on the paper roll and did not break the sealing wax. For the first time, she personally acknowledged the name of the second mate of the Seventh Boat — Han Bozhou, nicknamed "Sanlanzi"; the three rope scars on his left wrist were twisted out back when they crossed the Meisha rapids.

Liu Sanniang pointed out that the words “the seven-ship ledger is at Banhuchun” on the wax pill were meant for someone familiar to see—someone knew that she recognized ship plaques, and also knew Lu Wenfeng would send the thing to her. She further asserted that Banhuchun did not have that death-bringing ledger; if the ledger truly was in the building, then it was either a frame-up, or the insider from back then was still not dead.

Lu Wenfeng holds down Liu Sanniang’s hand as she is about to break the wax, points out that green sand mixed into the sealing wax is the old rule by which the grain-transport gang passes death notices, and advances the questioning from “identifying the person” to “besides Han Bozhou, who else back then knew you were at Banhuchun Inn”—turning “the mole” from speculation into a question that must be answered face to face, and pointing directly at Liu Sanniang’s deepest taboo.

Liu Sanniang does not struggle when her hand is held down; she withdraws her fingertips, covers the paper roll and the ebony boat token together with a handkerchief, and pushes them three inches away from the lamplight, pointing out the old rule of Qingsha sealing death notices: if it is opened too early, the messenger’s life-intent will be cut off halfway.

Regarding “who else knows you are at Banhuchun Inn,” Liu Sanniang gives the list of people who knew back then: Han Bozhou; Shen Qingshan, the former accountant of the Cao Gang (Iron Abacus, rumored to have died in Huaibei five years ago but with no corpse ever found); and Qin Zhaoshui, the old helmsman (stricken by stroke for seven years, unless someone is borrowing his name).

Liu Sanniang asserts that, apart from Han Bozhou, the person most worth investigating is Shen Qingshan—if Iron Abacus is still alive, he knows about the seventh boat and also about Banhuchun; if he is dead, then someone has taken his old accounts, old seals, and old favors to play ghost.

Liu Sanniang presses the window latch even tighter and asks Lu Wenfeng in return: who took this wax pellet from behind Han Bozhou’s teeth—did he take it out with his own hands, or did someone pass it into her hands?

Lu Wenfeng answers, “I took it out with my own hands”—the old boatman who fished up the body only touched the lapel and never saw the wax pill; from the time he took it out until he reached Banhuchun Inn, the chain of custody for the wax pill narrowed to him alone. He then releases Liu Sanniang’s hand, advancing the inquiry from “who wrote it” to “if Shen Qingshan is still alive, what old mark would be recognizable at a glance”—the investigation advances from “counting heads” to “finding a person.”

Liu Sanniang states three old identifying marks of Shen Qingshan: the horizontal callus on the inner side of his left thumb worn by abacus beads; that when working the abacus he favored the three fingers of his left hand, and when doing “two and five return to one” his middle finger would strike one extra time; a blue-black mole behind his right ear (“Qingshan carrying ink”); and that when writing the character “Shen,” the final dot always hooked back (because an old injury to his right wrist made his finishing stroke unable to close straight). She also wipes clean the water marks on the table with a handkerchief and arranges for Lu Wenfeng to rest tonight in the elegant room by the river; at daybreak, Afu will go to the river wharf to ask about the background of the old boatman from Wupeng Bay, while Lu Wenfeng will not show himself.

Lu Wenfeng puts the boat plaque and wax pellet away again, asks that they not alert the old boatman yet and only keep watch for now, and advances the questioning from “what marks does Shen Qingshan have” to “among those who have stayed at the inn recently, is there anyone who works an abacus with the left hand, or writes the character “Shen” with a hook”—feeding the already obtained identifying features back into an in-house screening. The investigation advances from “looking for someone” to “comparing within one’s own hall”.

Liu Sanniang opens the room accounts from nearly the past half month and recognizes a suspicious man who stayed at the inn three days ago: he claimed to be a silk merchant from Huaibei, had river mud on the soles of his shoes, used three fingers of his left hand to move the abacus when settling the bill and tapped an extra time with his middle finger, wrote the final stroke of the character "申" in the register with a hook like a fishhook, stayed only one night before leaving by the small rear-river dock, and before leaving had asked, "Are there any trunks left in storage by people from the old grain-transport gang?"—three identifying marks collide in one place, and the target takes shape in her own hall.

Liu Sanniang refuses that person’s probing with “Banhuchun only sends wine, not lives,” and sets the tempo: do not alarm the old boatman yet; only have A Fu go to the wharf tomorrow to buy fish while keeping an eye out. If “Shen He” really is Iron Abacus, then since he has asked about the trunks, it means he also does not know where the accounts are—he is looking, and so are we, but we cannot let him know we have already awakened.

Lu Wenfeng advances the questioning from “recognizing features” to “checking physical evidence and the scene”—he wants that page of accounts, wants to see the room that person stayed in, and wants to check whether that person touched any old objects in the shop before leaving, advancing the investigation from “comparing features” to “turning over physical evidence and verifying the scene.”

Liu Sanniang opens the account book and shows only the line for “Shen He,” making clear that Earth Room No. 3 is by the back river, with a small dock right below the window; he will stay one night, the room fee is one qian, dinner requires only plain rice, salted fish, and hot tea, and when settling the bill, his left hand will move the abacus while his middle finger taps once more than usual.

Liu Sanniang recognizes that the person touched two old objects—the old abacus on the counter that Shen Qingshan left behind when he bought the shop back then (the third bead from the far left has been reversed), and the old bronze boat lamp dismantled from an old boat at Qixia Ferry at the stairway corner (on the inner side of the lamp belly there is an extra shallow scratch like a “seven” and like a fishhook). She asserts that this is a mark left for an accomplice: “the route has been found”.

Liu Sanniang closes the account book, lowers the lamp shade, and takes Lu Wenfeng to see Di No. 3, laying down the rule: “Looking is looking; don’t go rummaging through the bedboards. Banhuchun Inn still has business to do.”

Lu Wenfeng rises and lifts his sword, setting the method of investigation: first look at Di-character No. 3; do not move either the abacus or the boat lantern—what he left behind may not necessarily have been meant for us to see, so first look for things in the room that correspond to “seven.”

paths.summary: Taking the opportunity to close the window in the private room by the river, the two of them advance the topic from “identifying Shen Qingshan’s features” to “turning over physical evidence, examining the site, and checking the marks left by Shen He”—Liu Sanniang spreads out that page of accounts, recognizes the hidden marks on the old abacus and the old copper boat lamp, and takes Lu Wenfeng to see Earth No. 3. plot_point: Regular customer Lu Wenfeng returns to the inn. Under the conditions that the hall is seventy percent full and only one Tian-class room remains, Liu Sanniang completes the full arrangement of reserving the room, ordering dishes, warming wine, quoting the price, and recording the account, and settles five qian and six wen (with one wen left as account credit).

Lu Wenfeng advances the topic from “is all still peaceful” to “old waves are rising again,” and asks Liu Sanniang whether any old members of the Canal Gang have recently come asking about Qixia Crossing.

Liu Sanniang does not answer directly; with “tea may be hot, but words should not be”, she lowers her voice, arranges for Lu Wenfeng to go upstairs and shut the window before speaking further, and offers half a piece of the truth: in the past month, a few old faces have been loitering by the river, asking indirect questions, as if probing how many people from that boat back then are still left.
Liu Sanniang reiterates the rule of “not selling to officials, not selling to the jianghu”, and in turn probes what Lu Wenfeng heard on the road.

Lu Wenfeng responds with “the dead have spoken”—three days ago, a corpse was recovered from Wupeng Bay, with the old boat plaques from that batch at Qixia Ferry hidden on the body; he proposes waiting until they finish eating and go upstairs to discuss it in detail, and uses “if you still recognize the old secret marks of the canal gang” to ask Liu Sanniang to reclaim her former identity.

Liu Sanniang catches the heavy words; first she raises her voice and orders Afu to light the lamps, test the window latches, and bring hot water, drawing the conversation in the front hall to a close, then personally pours wine and, with “using the dead to pass words to the living,” lays bare the purpose of the boat tag surfacing.

Liu Sanniang, for the first time, directly claims her old identity in the grain-transport gang—"I recognize the secret marks on the boat plaques"—and arranges to go upstairs after Lu Wenfeng finishes eating, using her taking the account book up as the pretext.
Liu Sanniang asks back in turn: Was this corpse aimed at Lu Wenfeng, or at the people from Qixia Ferry who didn’t die cleanly back then?

Lu Wenfeng reveals another piece of detail about the corpse—the three old cable scars on the left wrist, "as if from someone who survived on the boat back then"; he also proactively suggests "closing the door tightly first," and wants to go upstairs to show Liu Sanniang "something."

Liu Sanniang catches “three old cable wounds”, quietly agrees to go upstairs to eat, and orders A'Fu to watch the front hall, turn the stair lamp low, and stew ginger soup to be sent to the door, sealing off both the eyes and ears in the hall and the route upstairs.

Using the account book as a pretext, Liu Sanniang quietly laid down the rules to Lu Wenfeng: “do not ask where one comes from, and no drawing blades inside the building.” Then she went upstairs into the riverside private room, lit the lamp, shut the window, slid the bolt, carefully inspected the door crack, spread out the account book and set an abacus on it, adopting the posture of settling accounts, and asked Lu Wenfeng to take out that “one thing.”

Lu Wenfeng unfastens the sheath and takes out an item in the riverside private room, pushing the ebony boat token wrapped in oilcloth to Liu Sanniang—an old grain-transport seal on the front, a newly carved character “seven” on the back—and presses her about what was loaded on the seventh-ranked boat at Qixia Ferry that year.

Liu Sanniang turns the lampwick down, lifts the cloth through a handkerchief, verifies that the old grain-transport seal is genuine and that the hidden fish-tail mark is the mark for escorting internal cargo back then, and accepts the boat plaque.

Liu Sanniang for the first time explains the true cargo of Qixia Ferry’s seventh boat—three tin boxes (official silver, salt certificates, and private toll accounts), with a Mr. Qi, an accountant from the Grain Transport Supervision Office, hidden in the bottom of the cabin together with his tri-border draft register; she also points out that the fire was set to seize the accounts and silence him, and asserts that this tag is a death warrant.

Lu Wenfeng takes out the second piece of physical evidence—the wax-sealed paper roll taken from behind the corpse's teeth, with 'the seven boats' accounts are at Banhuchun Inn' written on it—drawing the fire of the old case to the lintel of Liu Sanniang's own inn, and questioning her face-to-face about the names of the three people with cable wounds.

Liu Sanniang pressed down on the paper roll and did not break the sealing wax. For the first time, she personally acknowledged the name of the second mate of the Seventh Boat — Han Bozhou, nicknamed "Sanlanzi"; the three rope scars on his left wrist were twisted out back when they crossed the Meisha rapids.

Liu Sanniang pointed out that the words “the seven-ship ledger is at Banhuchun” on the wax pill were meant for someone familiar to see—someone knew that she recognized ship plaques, and also knew Lu Wenfeng would send the thing to her. She further asserted that Banhuchun did not have that death-bringing ledger; if the ledger truly was in the building, then it was either a frame-up, or the insider from back then was still not dead.

Lu Wenfeng holds down Liu Sanniang’s hand as she is about to break the wax, points out that green sand mixed into the sealing wax is the old rule by which the grain-transport gang passes death notices, and advances the questioning from “identifying the person” to “besides Han Bozhou, who else back then knew you were at Banhuchun Inn”—turning “the mole” from speculation into a question that must be answered face to face, and pointing directly at Liu Sanniang’s deepest taboo.

Liu Sanniang does not struggle when her hand is held down; she withdraws her fingertips, covers the paper roll and the ebony boat token together with a handkerchief, and pushes them three inches away from the lamplight, pointing out the old rule of Qingsha sealing death notices: if it is opened too early, the messenger’s life-intent will be cut off halfway.

Regarding “who else knows you are at Banhuchun Inn,” Liu Sanniang gives the list of people who knew back then: Han Bozhou; Shen Qingshan, the former accountant of the Cao Gang (Iron Abacus, rumored to have died in Huaibei five years ago but with no corpse ever found); and Qin Zhaoshui, the old helmsman (stricken by stroke for seven years, unless someone is borrowing his name).

Liu Sanniang asserts that, apart from Han Bozhou, the person most worth investigating is Shen Qingshan—if Iron Abacus is still alive, he knows about the seventh boat and also about Banhuchun; if he is dead, then someone has taken his old accounts, old seals, and old favors to play ghost.

Liu Sanniang presses the window latch even tighter and asks Lu Wenfeng in return: who took this wax pellet from behind Han Bozhou’s teeth—did he take it out with his own hands, or did someone pass it into her hands?

Lu Wenfeng answers, “I took it out with my own hands”—the old boatman who fished up the body only touched the lapel and never saw the wax pill; from the time he took it out until he reached Banhuchun Inn, the chain of custody for the wax pill narrowed to him alone. He then releases Liu Sanniang’s hand, advancing the inquiry from “who wrote it” to “if Shen Qingshan is still alive, what old mark would be recognizable at a glance”—the investigation advances from “counting heads” to “finding a person.”

Liu Sanniang states three old identifying marks of Shen Qingshan: the horizontal callus on the inner side of his left thumb worn by abacus beads; that when working the abacus he favored the three fingers of his left hand, and when doing “two and five return to one” his middle finger would strike one extra time; a blue-black mole behind his right ear (“Qingshan carrying ink”); and that when writing the character “Shen,” the final dot always hooked back (because an old injury to his right wrist made his finishing stroke unable to close straight). She also wipes clean the water marks on the table with a handkerchief and arranges for Lu Wenfeng to rest tonight in the elegant room by the river; at daybreak, Afu will go to the river wharf to ask about the background of the old boatman from Wupeng Bay, while Lu Wenfeng will not show himself.

Lu Wenfeng puts the boat plaque and wax pellet away again, asks that they not alert the old boatman yet and only keep watch for now, and advances the questioning from “what marks does Shen Qingshan have” to “among those who have stayed at the inn recently, is there anyone who works an abacus with the left hand, or writes the character “Shen” with a hook”—feeding the already obtained identifying features back into an in-house screening. The investigation advances from “looking for someone” to “comparing within one’s own hall”.

Liu Sanniang opens the room accounts from nearly the past half month and recognizes a suspicious man who stayed at the inn three days ago: he claimed to be a silk merchant from Huaibei, had river mud on the soles of his shoes, used three fingers of his left hand to move the abacus when settling the bill and tapped an extra time with his middle finger, wrote the final stroke of the character "申" in the register with a hook like a fishhook, stayed only one night before leaving by the small rear-river dock, and before leaving had asked, "Are there any trunks left in storage by people from the old grain-transport gang?"—three identifying marks collide in one place, and the target takes shape in her own hall.

Liu Sanniang refuses that person’s probing with “Banhuchun only sends wine, not lives,” and sets the tempo: do not alarm the old boatman yet; only have A Fu go to the wharf tomorrow to buy fish while keeping an eye out. If “Shen He” really is Iron Abacus, then since he has asked about the trunks, it means he also does not know where the accounts are—he is looking, and so are we, but we cannot let him know we have already awakened.

Lu Wenfeng advances the questioning from “recognizing features” to “checking physical evidence and the scene”—he wants that page of accounts, wants to see the room that person stayed in, and wants to check whether that person touched any old objects in the shop before leaving, advancing the investigation from “comparing features” to “turning over physical evidence and verifying the scene.”

Liu Sanniang opens the account book and shows only the line for “Shen He,” making clear that Earth Room No. 3 is by the back river, with a small dock right below the window; he will stay one night, the room fee is one qian, dinner requires only plain rice, salted fish, and hot tea, and when settling the bill, his left hand will move the abacus while his middle finger taps once more than usual.

Liu Sanniang recognizes that the person touched two old objects—the old abacus on the counter that Shen Qingshan left behind when he bought the shop back then (the third bead from the far left has been reversed), and the old bronze boat lamp dismantled from an old boat at Qixia Ferry at the stairway corner (on the inner side of the lamp belly there is an extra shallow scratch like a “seven” and like a fishhook). She asserts that this is a mark left for an accomplice: “the route has been found”.

Liu Sanniang closes the account book, lowers the lamp shade, and takes Lu Wenfeng to see Di No. 3, laying down the rule: “Looking is looking; don’t go rummaging through the bedboards. Banhuchun Inn still has business to do.”

Lu Wenfeng rises and lifts his sword, setting the method of investigation: first look at Di-character No. 3; do not move either the abacus or the boat lantern—what he left behind may not necessarily have been meant for us to see, so first look for things in the room that correspond to “seven.”

plot_point: Regular customer Lu Wenfeng returns to the inn. Under the conditions that the hall is seventy percent full and only one Tian-class room remains, Liu Sanniang completes the full arrangement of reserving the room, ordering dishes, warming wine, quoting the price, and recording the account, and settles five qian and six wen (with one wen left as account credit).

Lu Wenfeng advances the topic from “is all still peaceful” to “old waves are rising again,” and asks Liu Sanniang whether any old members of the Canal Gang have recently come asking about Qixia Crossing.

Liu Sanniang does not answer directly; with “tea may be hot, but words should not be”, she lowers her voice, arranges for Lu Wenfeng to go upstairs and shut the window before speaking further, and offers half a piece of the truth: in the past month, a few old faces have been loitering by the river, asking indirect questions, as if probing how many people from that boat back then are still left.
Liu Sanniang reiterates the rule of “not selling to officials, not selling to the jianghu”, and in turn probes what Lu Wenfeng heard on the road.

Lu Wenfeng responds with “the dead have spoken”—three days ago, a corpse was recovered from Wupeng Bay, with the old boat plaques from that batch at Qixia Ferry hidden on the body; he proposes waiting until they finish eating and go upstairs to discuss it in detail, and uses “if you still recognize the old secret marks of the canal gang” to ask Liu Sanniang to reclaim her former identity.

Liu Sanniang catches the heavy words; first she raises her voice and orders Afu to light the lamps, test the window latches, and bring hot water, drawing the conversation in the front hall to a close, then personally pours wine and, with “using the dead to pass words to the living,” lays bare the purpose of the boat tag surfacing.

Liu Sanniang, for the first time, directly claims her old identity in the grain-transport gang—"I recognize the secret marks on the boat plaques"—and arranges to go upstairs after Lu Wenfeng finishes eating, using her taking the account book up as the pretext.
Liu Sanniang asks back in turn: Was this corpse aimed at Lu Wenfeng, or at the people from Qixia Ferry who didn’t die cleanly back then?

Lu Wenfeng reveals another piece of detail about the corpse—the three old cable scars on the left wrist, "as if from someone who survived on the boat back then"; he also proactively suggests "closing the door tightly first," and wants to go upstairs to show Liu Sanniang "something."

Liu Sanniang catches “three old cable wounds”, quietly agrees to go upstairs to eat, and orders A'Fu to watch the front hall, turn the stair lamp low, and stew ginger soup to be sent to the door, sealing off both the eyes and ears in the hall and the route upstairs.

Using the account book as a pretext, Liu Sanniang quietly laid down the rules to Lu Wenfeng: “do not ask where one comes from, and no drawing blades inside the building.” Then she went upstairs into the riverside private room, lit the lamp, shut the window, slid the bolt, carefully inspected the door crack, spread out the account book and set an abacus on it, adopting the posture of settling accounts, and asked Lu Wenfeng to take out that “one thing.”

Lu Wenfeng unfastens the sheath and takes out an item in the riverside private room, pushing the ebony boat token wrapped in oilcloth to Liu Sanniang—an old grain-transport seal on the front, a newly carved character “seven” on the back—and presses her about what was loaded on the seventh-ranked boat at Qixia Ferry that year.

Liu Sanniang turns the lampwick down, lifts the cloth through a handkerchief, verifies that the old grain-transport seal is genuine and that the hidden fish-tail mark is the mark for escorting internal cargo back then, and accepts the boat plaque.

Liu Sanniang for the first time explains the true cargo of Qixia Ferry’s seventh boat—three tin boxes (official silver, salt certificates, and private toll accounts), with a Mr. Qi, an accountant from the Grain Transport Supervision Office, hidden in the bottom of the cabin together with his tri-border draft register; she also points out that the fire was set to seize the accounts and silence him, and asserts that this tag is a death warrant.

Lu Wenfeng takes out the second piece of physical evidence—the wax-sealed paper roll taken from behind the corpse's teeth, with 'the seven boats' accounts are at Banhuchun Inn' written on it—drawing the fire of the old case to the lintel of Liu Sanniang's own inn, and questioning her face-to-face about the names of the three people with cable wounds.

Liu Sanniang pressed down on the paper roll and did not break the sealing wax. For the first time, she personally acknowledged the name of the second mate of the Seventh Boat — Han Bozhou, nicknamed "Sanlanzi"; the three rope scars on his left wrist were twisted out back when they crossed the Meisha rapids.

Liu Sanniang pointed out that the words “the seven-ship ledger is at Banhuchun” on the wax pill were meant for someone familiar to see—someone knew that she recognized ship plaques, and also knew Lu Wenfeng would send the thing to her. She further asserted that Banhuchun did not have that death-bringing ledger; if the ledger truly was in the building, then it was either a frame-up, or the insider from back then was still not dead.

Lu Wenfeng holds down Liu Sanniang’s hand as she is about to break the wax, points out that green sand mixed into the sealing wax is the old rule by which the grain-transport gang passes death notices, and advances the questioning from “identifying the person” to “besides Han Bozhou, who else back then knew you were at Banhuchun Inn”—turning “the mole” from speculation into a question that must be answered face to face, and pointing directly at Liu Sanniang’s deepest taboo.

Liu Sanniang does not struggle when her hand is held down; she withdraws her fingertips, covers the paper roll and the ebony boat token together with a handkerchief, and pushes them three inches away from the lamplight, pointing out the old rule of Qingsha sealing death notices: if it is opened too early, the messenger’s life-intent will be cut off halfway.

Regarding “who else knows you are at Banhuchun Inn,” Liu Sanniang gives the list of people who knew back then: Han Bozhou; Shen Qingshan, the former accountant of the Cao Gang (Iron Abacus, rumored to have died in Huaibei five years ago but with no corpse ever found); and Qin Zhaoshui, the old helmsman (stricken by stroke for seven years, unless someone is borrowing his name).

Liu Sanniang asserts that, apart from Han Bozhou, the person most worth investigating is Shen Qingshan—if Iron Abacus is still alive, he knows about the seventh boat and also about Banhuchun; if he is dead, then someone has taken his old accounts, old seals, and old favors to play ghost.

Liu Sanniang presses the window latch even tighter and asks Lu Wenfeng in return: who took this wax pellet from behind Han Bozhou’s teeth—did he take it out with his own hands, or did someone pass it into her hands?

Lu Wenfeng answers, “I took it out with my own hands”—the old boatman who fished up the body only touched the lapel and never saw the wax pill; from the time he took it out until he reached Banhuchun Inn, the chain of custody for the wax pill narrowed to him alone. He then releases Liu Sanniang’s hand, advancing the inquiry from “who wrote it” to “if Shen Qingshan is still alive, what old mark would be recognizable at a glance”—the investigation advances from “counting heads” to “finding a person.”

Liu Sanniang states three old identifying marks of Shen Qingshan: the horizontal callus on the inner side of his left thumb worn by abacus beads; that when working the abacus he favored the three fingers of his left hand, and when doing “two and five return to one” his middle finger would strike one extra time; a blue-black mole behind his right ear (“Qingshan carrying ink”); and that when writing the character “Shen,” the final dot always hooked back (because an old injury to his right wrist made his finishing stroke unable to close straight). She also wipes clean the water marks on the table with a handkerchief and arranges for Lu Wenfeng to rest tonight in the elegant room by the river; at daybreak, Afu will go to the river wharf to ask about the background of the old boatman from Wupeng Bay, while Lu Wenfeng will not show himself.

Lu Wenfeng puts the boat plaque and wax pellet away again, asks that they not alert the old boatman yet and only keep watch for now, and advances the questioning from “what marks does Shen Qingshan have” to “among those who have stayed at the inn recently, is there anyone who works an abacus with the left hand, or writes the character “Shen” with a hook”—feeding the already obtained identifying features back into an in-house screening. The investigation advances from “looking for someone” to “comparing within one’s own hall”.

Liu Sanniang opens the room accounts from nearly the past half month and recognizes a suspicious man who stayed at the inn three days ago: he claimed to be a silk merchant from Huaibei, had river mud on the soles of his shoes, used three fingers of his left hand to move the abacus when settling the bill and tapped an extra time with his middle finger, wrote the final stroke of the character "申" in the register with a hook like a fishhook, stayed only one night before leaving by the small rear-river dock, and before leaving had asked, "Are there any trunks left in storage by people from the old grain-transport gang?"—three identifying marks collide in one place, and the target takes shape in her own hall.

Liu Sanniang refuses that person’s probing with “Banhuchun only sends wine, not lives,” and sets the tempo: do not alarm the old boatman yet; only have A Fu go to the wharf tomorrow to buy fish while keeping an eye out. If “Shen He” really is Iron Abacus, then since he has asked about the trunks, it means he also does not know where the accounts are—he is looking, and so are we, but we cannot let him know we have already awakened.

Lu Wenfeng advances the questioning from “recognizing features” to “checking physical evidence and the scene”—he wants that page of accounts, wants to see the room that person stayed in, and wants to check whether that person touched any old objects in the shop before leaving, advancing the investigation from “comparing features” to “turning over physical evidence and verifying the scene.”

Liu Sanniang opens the account book and shows only the line for “Shen He,” making clear that Earth Room No. 3 is by the back river, with a small dock right below the window; he will stay one night, the room fee is one qian, dinner requires only plain rice, salted fish, and hot tea, and when settling the bill, his left hand will move the abacus while his middle finger taps once more than usual.

Liu Sanniang recognizes that the person touched two old objects—the old abacus on the counter that Shen Qingshan left behind when he bought the shop back then (the third bead from the far left has been reversed), and the old bronze boat lamp dismantled from an old boat at Qixia Ferry at the stairway corner (on the inner side of the lamp belly there is an extra shallow scratch like a “seven” and like a fishhook). She asserts that this is a mark left for an accomplice: “the route has been found”.

Liu Sanniang closes the account book, lowers the lamp shade, and takes Lu Wenfeng to see Di No. 3, laying down the rule: “Looking is looking; don’t go rummaging through the bedboards. Banhuchun Inn still has business to do.”

Lu Wenfeng rises and lifts his sword, setting the method of investigation: first look at Di-character No. 3; do not move either the abacus or the boat lantern—what he left behind may not necessarily have been meant for us to see, so first look for things in the room that correspond to “seven.”

At the same time, Liu Sanniang faces the appearing Shen Qingshan alone inside the building: inside the belly of the old copper boat-lamp, an extra roll of extremely fine paper has appeared (sealed with blue-green sand, half exposed in the copper seam), and the third bead from the left on the old abacus slides back by itself; she raises her voice to send A'fu away, circles out from behind the counter, stops three steps from the lamp, and throws “Back then, you moved one account wrong and burned the people of an entire ferry crossing” straight at the empty stairwell; in the shadow of the second floor, someone sighs softly, the voice aged and hoarse, yet still carrying the dry hardness of abacus beads—“Sanniang, your temper is still this fierce”. Liu Sanniang replies coldly, “Enough reminiscing. Step out and let me see behind your right ear”—the central figure in the old case is confirmed face-to-face, and the other party has already taken the first move to win trust, disturb old objects, and appear.

Shen Qingshan stepped down one stair from the shadow of the staircase; the lamplight revealed half a thin face, graying hair at the temples, his left hand tucked into his sleeve, and a blue-black mole at the hairline behind his right ear—Liu Sanniang recognized him to his face: “Shen Qingshan, twelve years without seeing you, and you still aren’t quite dead.”

Shen Qingshan uses three fingers of his left hand to flick an abacus in the air to prove his identity, throws out “If I meant to harm you, it would not be me who came tonight”, and explains: “The seven-boat accounts are not at Banhuchun Inn, but the key to opening the accounts is inside this boat lantern. Before Han Bozhou died, he only had time to pass on half a sentence; the other half is in my hands.”

Liu Sanniang throws back in Shen Qingshan’s face the three accounts of Han Bozhou’s death, the Earth-character No. 3 green-sand black wax, and transferring Lu Wenfeng away, refusing to reminisce; Shen Qingshan drops a copper piece engraved with a crooked “seven,” leaves the words “Tell Lu Wenfeng that what is waiting for him in the abandoned granary is not me, but an eye left behind by the person who set the fire back then,” and then departs calmly, leaving only a gust of damp river-mud air on the stairs.

Liu Sanniang does not pursue. Her fingertips press down on the copper piece, and toward the kitchen she calls in a low voice, “A-Fu, guard the door. Liu Sanniang: the person is right in front of her, and the words have been handed over, yet she can only stand three steps away, unable even to reach out and lift the cover of that boat lamp. paths.reasoning_trace: past: Lu Wenfeng is an old regular who has not come for half a year and has arrived travel-worn this time; Liu Sanniang was once a female escort for the Cao Gang in her early years, and in the old case of the burning of Qixia Ferry twelve years ago, her sworn brother died; to this day she suspects there was a mole. present: Liu Sanniang has personally checked the token, recognized the old Cao seal and the fishtail secret mark, explained the true cargo loaded on the seventh boat, acknowledged the name Han Bozhou and the three cable scars on the left wrist, counted out the list of those who knew the facts back then and pointed the spearhead at Shen Qingshan, given three identifiable old marks of Shen Qingshan, and in her own room ledger recognized a suspicious guest from three days ago (claiming to be a Huaibei silk merchant, using three fingers of his left hand to work the abacus and tapping once more with the middle finger, writing the character '申' with a returning hook on the final stroke, leaving by the small rear-river wharf, and asking about the Cao Gang's old stored trunks and cases). She further recognized that the man had touched two old objects and left a secret mark resembling both a 'seven' and a fishhook. In this turn, Shen Qingshan appeared in person, admitted his identity, threw out 'the key to opening the account is in the boat lamp' and 'what is waiting for Lu Wenfeng in the abandoned granary is one eye left behind by the arsonist,' left behind a copper piece engraved with 'seven,' and departed calmly; Lu Wenfeng confirmed outside the abandoned granary that he had been lured away, and decided to return to the shop. Both sides have already pushed the topic to the core of the old case and Liu Sanniang's own threshold, and have entered the stage of 'identifying the person face to face and obtaining physical evidence,' so there is a credible path for advancing the dialogue from 'identifying the person face to face' to 'opening the boat lamp, pursuing the accounts, pursuing the mole, and investigating the one eye left by the arsonist.'
requirements: Lu Wenfeng returns to Banhuchun Inn, meets up with Liu Sanniang, and exchanges what they saw outside the abandoned granary door and what Shen Qingshan explained in person.
Liu Sanniang and Lu Wenfeng jointly inspect the blue-green sandpaper roll inside the belly of the old copper boat lantern, or decide when and by what method to open the lantern and retrieve the item.
The copper piece engraved with “seven” left by Shen Qingshan and the clue that “the one waiting for Lu Wenfeng in the abandoned granary is an eye left by the arsonist” are being investigated.

The two sides reach a certain tacit understanding or division of labor on the next steps: watch Shen He, investigate Shen Qingshan’s whereabouts, check whether the account book is really in the shop, check whether Qin Zhaoshui’s name has been borrowed by someone, and investigate the one eye left behind by the arsonist.
paths.summary: Lu Wenfeng returns to Banhuchun Inn and meets up with Liu Sanniang. The two of them together examine the blue-sand paper scroll inside the old copper ship lamp, and follow up on the clue of the copper piece carved with “seven” left by Shen Qingshan and “one eye left by the arsonist”—the key to opening the accounts surfaces, and the whereabouts of the accounts and the identity of the mole draw closer; the old item Liu Sanniang has kept for twelve years is finally opened face to face, the relationship is reconnected, Liu Sanniang learns some of the movements, and Lu Wenfeng also gets hold of the thread.

original.rationale: In this turn, Liu Sanniang has already spoken aloud the core secret she has guarded for twelve years, the specific personal names, the list of those in the know, the identifying features, the background of the guests in her own establishment, and the hidden marks on old objects; there is no retreat left. Shen Qingshan appears in person and hands over key physical evidence and clues, and Lu Wenfeng comes with the corpse, the boat tag, and the wax pellet, originally for the purpose of reconciling accounts. Both sides have already pushed the conversation to the core, the physical evidence is in hand, and the stage has been set; the most likely course is to continue digging deeper along this path.

original.rationale: Under the rule of “no pursuing, no questioning” and Liu Sanniang’s measured discretion, if either side reins in the conversational thread, the dialogue stops at a perfectly proper exchange between familiar customers.

paths.label: Degrade

Both sides feel they cannot probe the depth of the next step and so close their mouths; the thread of talk stops, and both reminiscing and sounding out fall through, leaving only routine buying and selling.

original.rationale: The regular-customer relationship provides a buffer, but under the three words ‘Qixia Ferry,’ both sides are sensitive; if a private talk circles emptily around the core secret, the conversation may still stall.

paths.label: Collapse
paths.reasoning_trace: past: Lu Wenfeng arrives with unspoken worries and vigilance; Liu Sanniang has a deep taboo around the three words "Qixia Ferry," and the foundation of the inn's standing is "trust," with no blade-drawing allowed upstairs; present: Lu Wenfeng has already pursued with his sword to outside the abandoned granary, while Liu Sanniang is guarding the inn alone, and Shen Qingshan has already appeared in person and left. original.rationale: Lu Wenfeng has already pursued with his sword to outside the gate of the abandoned granary, Liu Sanniang is guarding the shop alone, and Shen Qingshan has appeared in person and then left. Both sides are in a state of high alert; if the black shadow turns back or blood is drawn, it may trigger a hard boundary or exposure event, making the interaction unable to continue.

evidence: Lu Wenfeng: “The wind chime didn’t ring; it was the dead who spoke. Three days ago, a corpse was fished up in Wupeng Bay, with that batch of old boat tags from Qixia Ferry hidden on the body.”
Lu Wenfeng: 'The wax pellet was taken from behind the corpse's teeth. On it there was only one sentence: "The accounts for the seven ships are at Banhuchun Inn."'
Lu Wenfeng: ‘Don’t dismantle it yet. The sealing wax is mixed with green sand; it’s an old canal-gang rule for conveying news of a death.’
Lu Wenfeng: “Aside from Han Bozhou, who else back then knew you were at Banhuchun Inn?”
Lu Wenfeng: “I took it out with my own hands. The old boatman who retrieved the corpse only touched the lapel and didn’t see the wax pellet; after I took it out, I came straight here to you.”
Lu Wenfeng: “If Shen Qingshan is still alive, what old mark would identify him at a glance?”

Lu Wenfeng: “Don't alarm the old boatman yet; just keep an eye on him. Think carefully: among the people who have stayed here recently, was there anyone who flicked the abacus with the left hand, or wrote the character ‘Shen’ with a hook?”

Lu Wenfeng: “Show me that page of his account and the room he stayed in. If he really is Iron Abacus, asking about the trunks was a feint; leaving a mark was the real point—and, before he left, did he touch any old objects in the inn?”
Lu Wenfeng: “Look at Room Dizi No. 3 first. Don’t touch the abacus or the ship lamp—what he left may not have been meant for us to see. First find the things in the room that correspond to ‘seven.’”
Lu Wenfeng: “Three knocks means I’m calling you; four knocks means I’ve already followed. If you hear four knocks, guard the shop and don’t chase—leave the old fish for me to identify.”
Lu Wenfeng: “Shen Qingshan, the accounts of the seven boats are not on me. If you still remember Han Bozhou, turn around and let me see behind your right ear.”
Lu Wenfeng: 'Moving me away from the shop—well played. If you still refuse to show yourself, I, Lu, will return to Banhuchun and acknowledge another fish.'

Lu Wenfeng: "I stop waiting, turn around, and hurry back along the original route. When I reach the rear wharf of Banhuchun, I first hide in the shadow of the eaves and scan the doors and windows, then knock softly three times: 'Sanniang, it's me. That fish in the shop—did it leave any scales behind?'"
Liu Sanniang: “The hidden marks on the boat plaques, I recognize them; the ones I can't recognize accurately, I also remember whom to ask.”

Liu Sanniang: “The second mate of the Seventh Boat, Han Bozhou, nicknamed ‘Three Cables.’ Three cable scars on his left wrist, twisted out back when they crossed the Meisha Rapids—I have seen those scars.”

Liu Sanniang: “The second one: Shen Qingshan, the old accountant of the Grain Transport Gang, nicknamed Iron Abacus. Shop deeds, silver notes, brokers’ guarantees—everything passed through his hands. Five years ago, rumor had it he died in Huaibei, but I never saw the body.”

Three days ago, there was a man who stayed here claiming to be a silk merchant from Huaibei … When he settled the bill, he complained that Afu was too slow with the abacus, and reached out to flick it twice himself—three fingers of his left hand, with the middle finger striking one extra time.

Liu Sanniang: “When he registered, what he wrote was not ‘Shen’ (沈), but ‘Shen’ (申), the shen of the shen hour; his name was Shen He. But that last stroke hooked back, like a fishhook reeling in the line.”
Liu Sanniang: 'The third bead from the far left was turned over backward by him—that's not a technique Afu could have done.'

Liu Sanniang: “There is an extra, very shallow scratch on the inner side of the lamp belly, like a ‘seven,’ and also like half a fishhook. If his hand was not merely idle, then he is telling someone—the road has been found.”
Liu Sanniang: “Understood. Three knocks, I come; four knocks, I guard the shop and don’t chase.”

Liu Sanniang: “Beside the wet mark, the old abacus had at some point been taken out from the hidden compartment in the counter and placed squarely on the first stair. The third bead from the left was flipped over.”
Liu Sanniang: “’All right.’ I said softly, ‘Lure the tiger away from the mountain.’”

Liu Sanniang: “‘Shen Qingshan,’ I speak toward the empty stairwell, my voice not loud, yet enough for those above and below the beams to hear. ‘If you truly are still alive, then don’t use a broken abacus to play ghost with me. Back then, you miscalculated one account and burned a whole ferry landing’s worth of people; now you still want to make a second calculation inside my Banhuchun?’”
Liu Sanniang: ‘“Cut the reminiscing.” I said coldly, “Step out and let me see behind your right ear.”’
Liu Sanniang: “Shen Qingshan, twelve years without seeing you, and you still aren’t quite dead.”
Shen Qingshan: ‘“Sanniang, if I meant to harm you, I would not be the one who came tonight.”’

Shen Qingshan: ““The Seven Ships ledger is not in Banhuchun Inn, but the key to opening the ledger is inside this ship lantern. Before he died, Han Bozhou only had time to pass on half a sentence; the other half is in my hands.””
Shen Qingshan: “Tell Lu Wenfeng that the one waiting for him in the abandoned granary is not me, but an eye left behind by the person who set the fire back then.”
Liu Sanniang: “Put the thing down,” I said. “The person may leave. Banhuchun will not keep blood tonight, nor will it keep your old life.”
Liu Sanniang: “I didn’t give chase. I only called in a low voice toward the kitchen: “Afu, guard the door. No one is allowed in, and no one is allowed out—wait until Lord Lu returns.””
Liu Sanniang: “I heard three knocks from behind the door. At first I did not open it; through the crack in the door, I asked in a low voice, ‘What was put in the soup?’”
Liu Sanniang: "'It left something behind.' I lower my voice extremely low and lead you toward the stairwell: 'One bright scale, one dark scale.'"

Liu Sanniang: “Minglin is there. Shen Qingshan left him behind with his own hands; I saw the blue mole behind his right ear, and the habit of using three fingers on his left hand to work the abacus hasn’t changed either—it’s him.”
Liu Sanniang: “‘The dark scale is in the belly of the lamp, a roll of paper, rolled up like a wick. I didn’t touch it. You said what’s left behind should be shown to you first.’”
Liu Sanniang: ““He also brought a message for you—the one waiting for you in the abandoned granary is not him, but an eye left behind by the person who set the fire back then.””
